messages.content: I want the goal to be speech–gesture reference resolution: the system should use gestures when they contribute to a reference, without confusing that contribution with correlations tied to a particular speaker. It also needs to work when the timing between speech and gesture is uncertain.

The distinction is between gesture-dependent meaning and speaker-specific correlations. For a reference whose meaning depends on a gesture, the gesture should help resolve what the speaker means. But a pattern associated with who is speaking should not be mistaken for the gesture’s contribution. Uncertain cross-modal timing matters because the relevant speech and gesture may not line up exactly.
How do I make the desired improvement explicit?

Set the target at an accuracy gain of at least 10 percentage points over speech-only models on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers. That names the comparison baseline, the kind of references on which the gain matters, and the condition that the speakers are unseen.
Is “10 percentage points” different from “10 percent” here?

Yes. Percentage points express an absolute difference in accuracy, not a relative percentage increase. The requirement is for at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models on the specified gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers.
Why keep “from unseen speakers” attached to that comparison?

Because the improvement is meant to hold on references from unseen speakers, not merely on references from speakers already encountered. That condition is important to the goal of distinguishing gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations. The requirement does not, by itself, prescribe how speakers are separated or how the comparison is carried out.
Could the gain be read as applying to every reference, even one that does not need a gesture?

No. The stated ≥10-percentage-point gain applies to gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers. It should not be broadened into a numerical gain requirement for every kind of reference. A gesture-dependent reference is one for which the gesture contributes to resolving what is being referred to.
I also want the system not to become fragile when a gesture is irrelevant.

The robustness requirement covers that: limit accuracy degradation to 5 percentage points under irrelevant-gesture substitutions. The point is that an irrelevant gesture should not cause a large drop in reference-resolution accuracy. This is a limit on degradation, separate from the requested gain over speech-only models.
And how should the timing part be stated without making it sound as though speech and gesture are perfectly synchronized?

State that accuracy degradation should also be limited to 5 percentage points under ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets. That preserves the explicit timing condition while acknowledging uncertainty in the alignment between what is heard and what is seen.
Does the plus-or-minus sign matter?

Yes. It expresses offsets in either direction, rather than only one direction of audiovisual misalignment. The requirement specifies ±300 milliseconds; it does not require choosing a sign convention for which stream leads the other.
So the accuracy gain and the degradation limit should not be collapsed into one number?

Right. They answer different questions. The ≥10-percentage-point gain compares accuracy with speech-only models on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers. The 5-percentage-point limit constrains accuracy degradation under irrelevant-gesture substitutions and ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets. Meeting one numerical condition would not, by itself, express the other.
When we say “distinguishes gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations,” are we requiring the system to ignore who is speaking altogether?

Not necessarily. The goal is narrower: it should not mistake correlations associated with a speaker for the meaning supplied by a gesture. The stated requirements focus on resolving gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers and retaining accuracy under the specified irrelevant-gesture and timing perturbations. They do not prescribe a blanket rule about all speaker information.
I want to avoid implying that any visible movement is automatically useful.

That fits the distinction. A gesture can contribute to a reference, but an irrelevant gesture should not be treated as though it resolves that reference. The irrelevant-gesture substitution condition makes that caution measurable through the limit of 5 percentage points of accuracy degradation.
Can I describe the timing uncertainty as simply a possible mismatch between the audio and visual cues?

Yes, as long as the explicit bound remains present. “Possible mismatch between audio and visual cues” conveys the general issue; “±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets” states the condition under which accuracy degradation is limited to 5 percentage points.
Would saying “robust to arbitrary delays” be equivalent?

No. Arbitrary delays would be a broader claim than the stated condition. The timing requirement names ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets. It does not establish a degradation limit for every possible delay.
Nor should I say the goal has already been achieved, correct?

Correct. This is a goal with performance requirements, not a report of an achieved result. The intended outcome is speech–gesture reference resolution that distinguishes gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations under uncertain cross-modal timing, with the specified accuracy gain and degradation limits.
Could you put it into one concise formulation while retaining every condition?

Enable speech–gesture reference resolution that distinguishes gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations under uncertain cross-modal timing. Achieve at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers, while limiting accuracy degradation to 5 percentage points under irrelevant-gesture substitutions and ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets.
For the model proposal, I want to train a speaker-adversarial, relevance-gated grounding model using counterfactual gesture substitutions and latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization.

That is a proposed way to address the speech–gesture reference-resolution goal, not a claim that the goal has been achieved. The speaker-adversarial aspect addresses speaker-specific correlations; the relevance gate addresses whether a gesture should contribute to grounding a reference; counterfactual gesture substitutions help make that distinction salient during training; and latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization addresses uncertainty about when speech and gesture correspond.
What does “grounding” mean in that sentence?

Here, grounding means connecting a spoken reference, with any relevant gestural contribution, to what it refers to. Calling it a grounding model keeps the focus on reference resolution rather than on recognizing gestures in isolation.
Does “speaker-adversarial” mean the model should disregard the speaker entirely?

Not necessarily. It means the proposed training should push against reliance on speaker-specific correlations when resolving references. That is different from claiming that all speaker information is removed or that speaker identity can never matter in another context.
And the relevance gate is there because not every gesture should affect the answer?

Yes. A relevance-gated model is meant to distinguish a gesture that contributes to a reference from one that does not. The gate expresses whether gesture information should influence grounding, without presuming that every visible gesture is useful.
How do counterfactual gesture substitutions fit with that gate?

They provide a proposed training signal for asking whether the interpretation depends on the gesture supplied. By considering a gesture substitution counterfactually, the model can be trained to distinguish a meaningful gestural contribution from an association that persists for other reasons. The proposal does not specify which gestures to substitute or an exact procedure for choosing them.
I do not want the wording to imply that changing a gesture must always change the reference.

It should not. Whether a substitution matters depends on whether the gesture is relevant to that reference. The relevance-gated part of the proposal is precisely about allowing gesture information to matter when it contributes meaning, while not treating every substitution as a reason to change the grounding.
Could I call the substitutions a way to test the importance of gesture during training?

As a conceptual description, yes: they let training consider how the grounding would behave with a different gesture. Keep it framed as the role of the proposed substitutions, though, rather than as a completed test or a demonstrated effect.
What is latent about the ±300-ms alignment?

The alignment is treated as an uncertain, unobserved choice rather than a single known correspondence between speech and gesture. “Latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization” means accounting for possible audiovisual alignments within that stated timing range when grounding the reference, instead of depending on one exact alignment.
Does marginalization mean committing to the offset that looks best?

No. Marginalization means accounting for uncertainty across possible alignments rather than making the result depend solely on one selected offset. The proposal names the ±300-ms range but does not specify the precise mathematical form used to represent or combine those possibilities.
So this is not a claim that the audiovisual offset is always exactly 300 milliseconds?
Correct. The ±300-ms notation describes a range in both timing directions. It does not say that every instance has an offset of 300 milliseconds, or prescribe which stream leads.
How do these parts relate without turning them into separate goals?

They are parts of one proposed training approach for a speech–gesture grounding model. Speaker-adversarial training targets reliance on speaker-specific correlations; relevance gating governs whether gesture information contributes; counterfactual gesture substitutions bear on that relevance distinction; and latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization accommodates timing uncertainty. Together they describe the proposal, not four independently established results.
Should I say this model will meet the accuracy requirements we discussed?

Not as a result. You can say the proposal is intended to support those requirements, but the node does not report accuracy measurements or show that the model meets them. Its content is the proposed training approach.
I also want to avoid smuggling in a particular architecture or loss function.

Then keep the description at the level stated: train a speaker-adversarial, relevance-gated grounding model using counterfactual gesture substitutions and latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization. Those terms identify the proposed roles of the components without committing to a particular architecture, loss formulation, or substitution procedure.
Can “speaker-adversarial” and “relevance-gated” coexist without being redundant?

Yes. They address different questions. Speaker-adversarial training concerns whether the grounding relies on speaker-specific correlations. Relevance gating concerns whether a gesture contributes to resolving the reference at hand. A model could face both questions at once, so the two descriptions are complementary rather than interchangeable.
And the timing term is not another kind of relevance gate?

Right. Relevance asks whether gesture information should contribute; alignment uncertainty asks when the potentially relevant gesture corresponds to the speech. Latent ±300-ms alignment marginalization addresses the latter without, by itself, deciding the former.
Give me a compact statement of the proposal that still sounds like a plan.

Propose training a speaker-adversarial, relevance-gated speech–gesture grounding model with counterfactual gesture substitutions and latent marginalization over ±300-ms audiovisual alignments. The intent is to ground gesture-dependent references without relying on speaker-specific correlations or a single assumed speech–gesture timing alignment.
The question I want to examine is whether speaker-adversarial training preserves referential gesture cues while relevance gating rejects distractors under ±300-ms alignment uncertainty.

That is the key open question for the proposed model. Speaker-adversarial training is intended to discourage reliance on speaker-specific correlations, but it should not erase gesture information needed to resolve a reference. Relevance gating is intended to keep distractor gestures from influencing the grounding. The question asks whether those two aims can hold together when speech and gesture may be misaligned by up to ±300 milliseconds; it does not assume that they do.
What exactly would it mean to preserve a referential gesture cue?

It would mean that, when a gesture contributes to identifying the referent, the model can still use that contribution. The concern is that suppressing speaker-specific correlations might also suppress useful information if the two are not adequately distinguished. Whether the proposed training avoids that problem remains a question.
And “rejects distractors” does not mean rejecting all gestures?

Correct. A distractor is a gesture that should not determine the reference at hand. The proposed relevance gate is meant to prevent such a gesture from driving the grounding, while still allowing a referential gesture to contribute. The question is whether it makes that distinction successfully.
Why include the ±300-ms alignment uncertainty in the same question?

Because uncertainty about when a gesture corresponds to speech can complicate the relevance judgment. The question is not merely whether the model distinguishes useful gestures from distractors when timing is clear; it asks whether that distinction holds under ±300-ms alignment uncertainty.
Does ±300 ms imply that the gesture must come after the speech?
No. The plus-or-minus notation allows offsets in either direction. The question does not specify which stream leads, only that alignment is uncertain within the stated ±300-ms condition.
Could speaker-adversarial training look helpful in one respect but still make the gesture cue harder to use?

That is precisely the tension the question raises. Reducing dependence on speaker-specific correlations and retaining referential gesture cues are distinct aims. The wording asks whether both can be achieved, rather than treating success on one as proof of success on the other.
Is relevance gating being asked to resolve the timing uncertainty by itself?

Not by itself. The question concerns relevance gating under alignment uncertainty: can it reject distractors when the timing between modalities is uncertain? It does not say that gating alone estimates alignment or specify how timing uncertainty is handled internally.
I want the question to stay about the interaction, not become two unrelated questions.

Then keep the word “while” doing real work: does speaker-adversarial training preserve referential gesture cues while relevance gating rejects distractors, with both considered under ±300-ms alignment uncertainty? That asks whether the intended behaviors coexist in the same setting, rather than assuming that either one guarantees the other.
Could I phrase it as though the proposed model has already proved that balance?

That would change the meaning. This node poses an open question, not a finding. It is appropriate to ask whether the balance holds; it would not be faithful to say that referential cues have been preserved or distractors have been rejected.
What should I avoid implying about a distractor gesture?

Avoid implying that every gesture is a distractor or that a gesture is irrelevant solely because its timing is uncertain. The question separates two issues: whether the gesture contributes to the reference and whether its alignment with speech is uncertain within ±300 milliseconds.
Similarly, should I avoid assuming that a cue is speaker-specific just because it accompanies one speaker?

Yes. The question depends on distinguishing a cue’s referential contribution from a speaker-specific correlation. It does not establish that any particular cue belongs to one category or the other. The concern is whether the proposed training preserves the former while pushing against reliance on the latter.
Can you restate the question without losing any of those distinctions?

Under ±300-ms uncertainty in speech–gesture alignment, does speaker-adversarial training retain gesture cues that genuinely help resolve a reference, while relevance gating prevents distractor gestures from influencing that resolution? This remains a question about the proposed approach, not a reported outcome.
So if I ask whether it works, I need to mean both preservation and rejection under that timing condition?

Exactly. “Works” would otherwise be too broad. Here the issue is specifically whether referential gesture cues remain usable despite speaker-adversarial training and whether the relevance gate rejects distractors, both under ±300-ms alignment uncertainty. Neither behavior should be presumed from the proposal alone.

My hypothesis is that, on unseen speakers, adversarial alignment-marginalized gating beats speech-only by at least 10 accuracy points, while irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms offsets cost no more than 5 accuracy points.

That states a predicted outcome, not an observed one. It pairs a gain of at least 10 percentage points over speech-only on unseen speakers with an accuracy-loss limit of at most 5 percentage points under irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms audiovisual offsets. Together, those predictions speak to whether useful gestural information can be retained without making reference resolution overly sensitive to distractors or timing uncertainty.
Does the comparison with speech-only apply to the accuracy gain or to the 5-point cost as well?

The speech-only comparison is explicit for the predicted gain: adversarial alignment-marginalized gating is hypothesized to exceed speech-only accuracy by at least 10 percentage points on unseen speakers. The 5-point figure describes a limit on accuracy lost under irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms offsets; it should not be restated as a second comparison with speech-only.
Would it be accurate to say the model has shown a 10-point improvement?
No. The hypothesis says it will beat speech-only by at least 10 accuracy points in the stated setting. It provides no measured accuracy or completed result.
Why is the unseen-speaker condition important to keep in the hypothesis?

It specifies where the predicted gain must hold. In the context of speaker-adversarial training, an improvement on unseen speakers is pertinent to the concern about speaker-specific correlations. But the hypothesis does not establish that those correlations have actually been removed.
When I say “adversarial alignment-marginalized gating,” am I describing the whole proposed approach rather than claiming that any one component causes the gain?

Yes. The phrase names the proposed approach as a whole: an adversarial aspect concerning speaker-specific correlations, gating concerning gesture relevance, and marginalization concerning uncertain alignment. The hypothesis predicts performance for that approach; it does not assign a measured share of the predicted gain to any one component.
How does this hypothesis address the question about preserving referential gesture cues?

The predicted advantage over speech-only on unseen speakers is consistent with the model making useful use of information beyond speech, including referential gestures. That is why it bears on the preservation question. Accuracy alone, however, would not by itself prove precisely how the model used a particular gesture cue.
And does the 5-point limit address the distractor side of the question?

It gives a performance expectation for that side: irrelevant gestures should cost no more than 5 percentage points of accuracy. That is compatible with successfully limiting distractor influence, but the hypothesis remains a prediction about accuracy, not an established account of what the relevance gate does internally.
I also mean the timing condition to be part of the robustness prediction.

It is. The hypothesis predicts an accuracy cost of no more than 5 percentage points under ±300-ms audiovisual offsets. The plus-or-minus notation matters: the stated timing uncertainty allows offsets in either direction, without saying which stream leads.
Does that mean the system is predicted to tolerate any amount of misalignment?
No. The timing condition stated here is ±300 milliseconds. The hypothesis does not make a claim about arbitrary offsets beyond that condition.
Could someone read “irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms offsets” as a guarantee about both perturbations occurring together?

The wording names two robustness conditions: irrelevant gestures and ±300-ms offsets. It does not separately state a bound for their simultaneous combination. It is safest to retain the stated conditions rather than infer an additional combined-perturbation guarantee.
Are the 10 points and 5 points relative percentage changes?

No. They are accuracy points, conventionally expressed as percentage points. The hypothesis predicts an absolute accuracy difference of at least 10 percentage points against speech-only and an absolute accuracy loss of at most 5 percentage points under the named perturbations; neither figure denotes a relative percent change.
If the 5-point cost holds, can I automatically say the model still beats speech-only by at least 10 points when there is an irrelevant gesture?

No. The ≥10-point advantage and the ≤5-point cost are distinct predictions. The hypothesis does not explicitly state the model’s margin over speech-only under an irrelevant gesture or a timing offset, so the original ≥10-point comparison should not be carried over unchanged to those conditions.
Should the hypothesis say that the gate always identifies the right gesture?

No. It predicts aggregate accuracy relationships, not perfect identification of relevant gestures. A limit of 5 percentage points on accuracy loss does not mean there can be no mistakes, and a gain over speech-only does not mean every referential cue is preserved in every instance.
Could the accuracy pattern alone establish that speaker-adversarial training, rather than gating or alignment marginalization, is responsible?

No. The hypothesis concerns the combined adversarial alignment-marginalized gating approach. Even if the predicted accuracy pattern were observed, attributing it specifically to one component would be a separate conclusion not stated here.
So how should I frame the relationship to the open question?

Frame this as a testable prediction bearing on the question: on unseen speakers, the proposed approach is expected to outperform speech-only by at least 10 accuracy points, while accuracy loss under irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms offsets is expected to be no more than 5 points. Those outcomes would be relevant to preserving referential gesture cues and resisting distractors under timing uncertainty, without treating the outcomes as already established or as proof of a particular internal mechanism.
Can you give me a single sentence that keeps the hypothesis status clear?

I hypothesize that, on unseen speakers, adversarial alignment-marginalized gating will exceed speech-only accuracy by at least 10 percentage points, while irrelevant gestures or ±300-ms audiovisual offsets will reduce its accuracy by no more than 5 percentage points.

To examine the question, I plan to build speaker-disjoint, 30-speaker ReferGesture-1K and compare speech-only, full, adversarial-free, and gate-free models on gesture-dependent, swapped-gesture, and ±300-ms-offset trials.

That is a comparison plan, not a report of results. The speaker-disjoint, 30-speaker ReferGesture-1K provides the planned setting. Comparing the four model variants across the three named trial conditions is intended to examine whether the full approach uses referential gestures, resists misleading gesture information, and handles uncertain speech–gesture timing.
What does “speaker-disjoint” contribute to the plan?

It means the speaker sets are kept separate across the relevant data partitions, so the comparison can address performance involving unseen speakers rather than relying on overlap in speaker identities. The plan does not specify the sizes of those partitions or how the 30 speakers are allocated among them.
Should I interpret “ReferGesture-1K” as a detailed specification of the dataset?

No. ReferGesture-1K is the dataset name in the plan, and the node explicitly says it is to be built with 30 speakers and speaker-disjoint partitions. It does not specify its recordings, annotation scheme, trial counts, or what the name’s “1K” denotes.
I want the comparison to include speech-only as well as the gesture-using models. Why is that distinction useful here?

Speech-only provides a comparison without gesture input. The full model represents the proposed approach with its named components, while the adversarial-free and gate-free variants allow comparisons involving the absence of each named component. The plan calls for comparing them; it does not presume which will perform better.
Would it be fair to call adversarial-free and gate-free ablations?

Yes, in the general sense that each omits a named part of the full approach: the adversarial aspect in one case and the relevance gate in the other. The plan does not specify any other differences in architecture or training, so it is best not to fill those in.
Does the adversarial-free comparison, by itself, prove whether speaker-specific correlations are present?

No. It is a planned comparison relevant to the role of speaker-adversarial training, especially in a speaker-disjoint setting. A difference between variants would be informative, but the plan alone supplies neither results nor a complete explanation of what information a model relies on.
And the gate-free variant is there to examine relevance gating rather than timing marginalization?

It is the variant named for omitting the gate, so it is relevant to the gate’s role. The plan does not specify a separate alignment-marginalization-free variant. It would therefore be inaccurate to describe this comparison as directly isolating every component of the proposed approach.
What role do gesture-dependent trials play?

They focus the comparison on references for which a gesture contributes to resolution. That makes them pertinent to the question of whether speaker-adversarial training preserves useful referential gesture cues. The plan does not say what outcomes those trials will produce.
Are swapped-gesture trials the same thing as gesture-dependent trials?

They name different conditions. “Gesture-dependent” describes references for which the gesture matters to resolution; “swapped-gesture” describes trials in which the gesture has been substituted. The plan includes both, but it does not specify that every swapped gesture is irrelevant or that every swap must change the correct interpretation.
So I should not simply label all swapped gestures as distractors?

Right. Swapped-gesture trials are relevant to whether the model responds appropriately when gesture information changes, including the concern about distractors. But the plan does not characterize every substitution as a distractor or state how each substitution affects the reference.
How should I describe the offset trials?

Call them ±300-ms-offset trials. They introduce the stated audiovisual timing uncertainty into the comparison. The plus-or-minus sign preserves offsets in either direction; the plan does not say which stream leads in a particular trial or specify other offset magnitudes.
Does listing the three trial types mean there are three separate datasets?

Not necessarily. The plan names ReferGesture-1K and three kinds of trials on which to compare the models. It does not specify whether those conditions are organized as separate datasets, subsets, or another arrangement.
Do we know how many trials each condition contains?
No. The plan specifies the speaker count, the dataset name, the four model variants, and the three trial conditions, but it does not give trial counts for any condition.
Would saying the full model has already beaten speech-only fit this node?
No. This node proposes building ReferGesture-1K and conducting model comparisons. It reports no completed comparisons or measured performance, so any ranking of the models would be premature.
How does the whole plan bear on the question about preserving cues while rejecting distractors?

The gesture-dependent trials make preservation of referential gesture information relevant to the comparison. Swapped-gesture trials bring changed gesture information into view, and ±300-ms-offset trials bring timing uncertainty into view. Comparing the full model with speech-only, adversarial-free, and gate-free variants in a speaker-disjoint setting is a way to investigate how those concerns coexist, without assuming the answer.
Can I say the design separately isolates the effect of timing marginalization?

Not on the information given. The plan lists offset trials, so timing robustness is part of what can be compared, but it does not name a model variant that removes alignment marginalization. Avoid claiming that this design separately isolates that component.
Should the plan say which model will win on swapped-gesture trials?
No. Naming the comparisons and trial conditions is enough for a plan. Predicting a winner would be a hypothesis; reporting one would require results. Neither is part of this node’s stated plan.
Could you restate the plan in one sentence without adding those assumptions?
Build speaker-disjoint, 30-speaker ReferGesture-1K, then compare speech-only, full, adversarial-free, and gate-free models on gesture-dependent, swapped-gesture, and ±300-ms-offset trials.
For the activity, train four models on 24 ReferGesture-1K speakers and measure accuracy on six held-out speakers under gesture-dependent, irrelevant-substitution, and ±300-ms-offset conditions.

That specifies the training and measurement activity without reporting an outcome. The four models are the speech-only, full, adversarial-free, and gate-free variants. All four are trained using the 24-speaker portion, and accuracy is measured on the six held-out speakers under each named condition.
Does “held-out” make the six speakers unseen for this comparison?

Yes. The distinction is between the 24 speakers used for training and the six speakers held out for accuracy measurement. Keeping those speaker groups separate makes the measurement about performance on speakers not included in training.
Is the total still 30 speakers?
Yes. The activity specifies 24 training speakers and six held-out speakers from ReferGesture-1K, for 30 speakers in those two groups. It does not give a further breakdown within either group.
I want to be precise about what is measured. Is it the accuracy of each model on the held-out speakers?

That is the stated measurement: accuracy for the four models on the six held-out speakers, under the gesture-dependent, irrelevant-substitution, and ±300-ms-offset conditions. No accuracy values are supplied yet.
Why keep the gesture-dependent condition distinct from the other two?

It asks how accurately the models resolve references that depend on a gesture. The irrelevant-substitution condition instead concerns accuracy when an irrelevant gesture is substituted, and the ±300-ms-offset condition concerns accuracy when audiovisual timing is offset. Naming them separately avoids treating gesture use, gesture irrelevance, and timing uncertainty as the same test.
Does “irrelevant-substitution” mean every possible gesture swap?

No. This activity specifically names irrelevant-substitution trials: the substituted gesture is irrelevant to the reference. That is narrower than saying that every possible gesture substitution is irrelevant.
And should I say the substituted gesture necessarily changes the correct referent?

No. Calling the substitution irrelevant does not establish a change in the correct referent. The activity is to measure accuracy under that substitution condition, without adding an unstated rule about how each reference must change.
What does the ±300-ms condition specify here?

It specifies audiovisual offsets of plus or minus 300 milliseconds as a condition for measuring accuracy on the held-out speakers. The sign allows timing displacement in either direction; the activity does not say which modality leads in a given trial.
Is that a claim about arbitrary audiovisual delays?
No. The named condition is ±300 milliseconds. The activity does not specify measurements at other offset magnitudes or support a claim about arbitrary delays.
Do the four models need to be listed every time I describe the measurement?

You can say “four models” once their identities are clear. If the description needs to stand alone, naming speech-only, full, adversarial-free, and gate-free makes the comparison unambiguous without adding new variants.
What is the speech-only model doing in an activity with gesture substitutions?

It remains one of the four accuracy comparisons. Because it uses speech alone, it provides a baseline alongside models that can use gesture information. Its inclusion does not imply that a gesture substitution changes its input or its accuracy.
Can these measurements bear on the prediction about unseen speakers without being described as results?

Yes. Training on 24 speakers and measuring on six held-out speakers sets up an unseen-speaker accuracy comparison. The gesture-dependent and robustness conditions make the measurements relevant to the predicted gain and accuracy-loss limits. The activity itself does not say whether any model meets those limits.
Should I infer from the activity that the full model beats the adversarial-free or gate-free model?
No. The activity calls for training and measuring all four variants. It gives no measured accuracies or ranking, so it cannot establish an advantage for the full model over either variant.
Nor does the activity alone tell us whether adversarial training preserves a particular gesture cue, right?

Right. Accuracy under the named conditions can inform that question, especially through comparisons among the variants, but the activity does not report results or identify what information any model used for a particular reference.
Does listing three conditions say whether they are applied separately or combined in the same trial?

It lists gesture-dependent, irrelevant-substitution, and ±300-ms-offset conditions for accuracy measurement. It does not specify a combined irrelevant-substitution-plus-offset condition, so that should not be added to the activity as though it were stated.
Could I specify a number of trials for each condition?
Not from this activity. It gives the speaker counts, model count, accuracy measure, and conditions, but no trial counts or allocation of trials among those conditions.
What if I phrase it as “the models were trained and achieved robust accuracy”?

That would add an unsupported outcome. You can describe the activity as training four models and measuring their accuracy on six held-out speakers; you cannot infer robust accuracy, an improvement, or a limited drop from the activity statement alone.
Can you give me a clean version that keeps the action and measurement together?

Train the speech-only, full, adversarial-free, and gate-free models on 24 ReferGesture-1K speakers, then measure each model’s accuracy on six held-out speakers under gesture-dependent, irrelevant-substitution, and ±300-ms audiovisual-offset conditions.
On held-out ReferGesture-1K speakers, gesture-dependent accuracy was 76% versus speech-only’s 68%, and irrelevant substitutions cost 7 points. How should I state that evidence?

State the two observations directly: gesture-dependent accuracy on held-out ReferGesture-1K speakers was 76%, compared with 68% for speech-only, and irrelevant substitutions cost 7 accuracy points. These are measured outcomes, not predictions.
What is the observed difference between 76% and 68%?
It is 8 percentage points of accuracy. That is an absolute difference between the two reported accuracies, not an 8% relative increase.
Should I say the 7-point cost is a 7% relative decline?
No. The evidence says irrelevant substitutions cost 7 points, so describe it as a 7-percentage-point accuracy cost. It does not state a relative percentage decline.
Can I calculate the accuracy under irrelevant substitutions by subtracting seven from 76?

Not from this statement alone. It gives the cost of irrelevant substitutions but does not explicitly identify the reference accuracy from which that cost was calculated. Reporting a substituted-condition accuracy would add a number the evidence does not supply.
Is the 76% figure specifically about gesture-dependent references?

Yes. The 76% and the speech-only comparison of 68% are reported for gesture-dependent accuracy on held-out ReferGesture-1K speakers. They should not be presented as accuracies for every trial condition.
Does “held-out speakers” matter to how I describe the result?

Yes. It identifies the speaker condition under which these outcomes were observed. Keep that qualification attached to the evidence rather than describing the figures as unrestricted ReferGesture-1K accuracies.
Can I attribute the 8-point difference specifically to the speaker-adversarial component?

No. The reported figures establish the difference between gesture-dependent accuracy and speech-only accuracy on the held-out speakers. They do not isolate how much of that difference is attributable to speaker-adversarial training, relevance gating, or alignment handling.
What about saying the irrelevant-substitution result shows the gate rejected distractors?

That would go beyond the reported observation. The evidence gives a 7-point accuracy cost under irrelevant substitutions; it does not directly establish how the gate treated each substituted gesture or what caused the cost.
Do we have an accuracy figure for the ±300-ms-offset condition in this evidence?
No. This evidence reports the held-out-speaker gesture-dependent comparison and the cost of irrelevant substitutions. It supplies no accuracy or accuracy cost for ±300-ms audiovisual offsets.
So I should not combine the irrelevant-substitution cost with the offset condition?
Correct. The reported 7-point cost is for irrelevant substitutions. It is not stated as the cost of ±300-ms offsets or as the cost when substitutions and offsets occur together.
Would “gesture-dependent accuracy improved by 8 points” be clear enough?

It is clearer if you include the comparator and setting: on held-out ReferGesture-1K speakers, gesture-dependent accuracy was 8 percentage points higher than speech-only, at 76% versus 68%. That makes the observed comparison explicit without implying a broader result.
Is the 7-point cost another comparison against speech-only?

The evidence does not say that. Speech-only’s 68% is the explicit comparator for the 76% gesture-dependent accuracy. The irrelevant-substitution statement reports an accuracy cost but does not name speech-only as its comparator.
Can I describe these as two findings rather than one overall accuracy figure?
